UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                 BEFORE THE
                   FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


    PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                       )          Docket No. ER26-3525-000


             MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND LIMITED ANSWER
                      OF PJM INTERCONNECTION, L.L.C.

           PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) hereby submits this Motion for Leave to

Answer and Answer (“Answer”)1 to the protest and comments of the Towering Concerns,

LLC (“Towering Concerns”)2 in response to PJM’s August 14, 2026 filing3 in this docket,

in which PJM submitted revisions to Tariff, Schedule 12-Appendix A to incorporate cost

responsibility assignments for baseline upgrades in the recent update to the Regional

Transmission Expansion Plan (“RTEP”) approved by the PJM Board of Managers (“PJM

Board”) on July 15, 2026.

           Towering Concerns makes specific allegations regarding baseline upgrades

b4000.344 and b4000.345 (the “Thornburg Project”) that were approved by the PJM Board

and incorporated into the RTEP in February 2025, and for which the Commission accepted

cost responsibility assignments in May 2025.4 Towering Concerns raises a number of

issues with the Thornburg Project, including description, need, site control, routing, local

Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“Commission”). 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212, 385.213.
2
  PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Protest and Comments of Towering Concerns, LLC Regarding Federal

3
  PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Revisions to Incorporate Cost Responsibility Assignments for Regional

set forth in the Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”), or in the August RTEP Cost Assignment Filing.

    See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 191 FERC ¶ 61,156 (2025).
 impacts, and other aspects of project development.5 As demonstrated below, these issues

are outside the scope of this proceeding, which solely concerns whether PJM correctly

calculated the proposed cost responsibility assignments in accordance with its Tariff. Thus,

the Commission can easily dismiss Towering Concerns’ Protest. Further, even if Towering

Concerns’ issues were within scope, they lack merit. To this end, PJM responds to three

points concerning: (i) the reliability basis for the Thornburg Project and its scope change;

(ii) the description of the Thornburg Project; and (iii) PJM’s assessment of need through

the RTEP process.

           Accordingly, and for the reasons set forth in more detail below, PJM respectfully

requests that the Commission: (i) grant this motion for leave to answer; (ii) reject the

arguments set forth in the Towering Concerns Protest; and (iii) accept the cost

responsibility assignments reported in the August RTEP Cost Assignment Filing, effective

November 12, 2026.

I.         MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER

           PJM respectfully requests leave to file this Answer to address arguments raised in

the Towering Concerns Protest.          Although the Commission’s Rules of Practice and

Procedure generally do not permit an answer to protests,6 the Commission routinely allows

such answers when they provide useful or relevant information that will assist the

Commission in its decision-making process, clarify the issues, assure a complete record in

the proceeding, provide information helpful to the disposition of an issue, and/or permit




5
  See Towering Concerns Protest at 4-7 (Scope, Description, and Location), 7-16 (Site Control), 16-18
(Project Need).
6
    18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(2).



                                                 2
 the issues to be narrowed.7 This Answer satisfies these standards, because it will help

clarify that the issues raised by Towering Concerns as outside the scope of this proceeding

and will correct the record. Accordingly, PJM respectfully submits that good cause exists

to grant this motion for leave to answer.

II.     BACKGROUND

        The Thornburg Project was initially identified by PJM as a solution to address the

reliability criteria violations identified as part of the 2024 RTEP Window 1 process. PJM’s

2024 RTEP Window 1 studies identified widespread voltage and thermal reliability criteria

violations under forecasted system conditions. Those included low voltage conditions and

transmission overloads associated with the power transfers needed to serve projected load

growth. The violations were not confined to a single locality or customer request, and PJM

selected a coordinated set of transmission reinforcements to address them. The Thornburg

Project—formerly referred to as the Kraken loop and the Kraken Substation—was among

the projects identified through the 2024 RTEP Window 1 process. The Thornburg Project

addresses, among other needs, stability restrictions affecting major generation facilities in

the area and reliability violations on Virginia Electric and Power Company’s (d/b/a

“Dominion Energy Virginia”) (“Dominion”) 500 kilovolts (“kV”) and 230 kV systems,

while providing transmission reinforcement along the I-95 and Fredericksburg corridors as



7
  See, e.g., Pioneer Transmission, LLC v. N. Ind. Pub. Serv. Co., 140 FERC ¶ 61,057, at P 94 (2012); Midwest
Indep. Transmission Sys. Operator, Inc., 131 FERC ¶ 61,285, at P 6 n.10 (2010); Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 131
FERC ¶ 61,252, at P 19 (2010) (accepting answers that “provided information that assisted [the Commission]
in [its] decision-making process”); Duke Energy Ky., Inc., 122 FERC ¶ 61,182, at P 25 (2008) (accepting
answers in proceeding that “provided information that assisted [the Commission] in [its] decision-making
process”); Tallgrass Transmission, LLC, 125 FERC ¶ 61,248, at P 26 (2008); Midwest Indep. Transmission
Sys. Operator, Inc., 120 FERC ¶ 61,083, at P 23 (2007) (answer to protests permitted when it provides
information to assist the Commission in its decision-making process); Morgan Stanley Cap. Grp., Inc. v. N.Y.
Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 93 FERC ¶ 61,017, at 61,036 (2000) (accepting an answer that was “helpful in the
development of the record.”).



                                                     3
 load grows. The Thornburg Project was approved by the PJM Board for inclusion in the

RTEP in February 2025 and Dominion was assigned construction responsibility.8

            Following discussions with Dominion, in May 2026, PJM presented to the

Transmission Expansion Advisory Committee (“TEAC”) a scope change related to the

Thornburg Project.9 The scope change did not create a new project or replace the reliability

need for which it was selected. Rather, it added 230 kV underbuild capability to the

transmission solution.         As described in the TEAC materials, this added capability

introduces efficiencies through allowing reuse of existing structure, minimizing future

environmental impacts and long-term capital costs, avoiding extended outages on critical

500 kV facilities, and allowing direct connectivity to load as it materializes in the area.10

The PJM Board approved the scope change in July 2026.11

III.        ANSWER

            A.        The Arguments Raised in the Towering Concerns Protest and Comments
                      Are Outside the Scope of this Proceeding

            Tariff, Schedule 12(b)(viii) requires that, within 30 days of PJM Board approval of

any update to the RTEP, PJM must submit a Tariff filing and a report with the Commission

setting forth the cost responsibility assignments for transmission enhancement and


8

at 207-08.
9
  Wenzheng Qiu, et al., Transmission Expansion Advisory Committee, Reliability Analysis Update, PJM
Interconnection, L.L.C. (May 8, 2026), 14-15, https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-
groups/committees/teac/2026/20260508/20260508-item-10---reliability-analysis-update.pdf
[https://perma.cc/6NBC-4LEV] (“May 2026 TEAC Presentation”).

groups/committees/teac/2026/20260707/20260707-pjm-board-whitepaper.pdf     [https://perma.cc/7GLC-
MW9C].

 expansion projects selected in PJM’s RTEP.12 The Commission has consistently held that

its review of such filings is limited to “whether PJM followed its Tariff provisions in

allocating cost responsibility according to its Tariff,”13 and has rejected arguments

challenging the justness and reasonableness of Commission-accepted cost allocation

methodologies and PJM’s implementation of its planning process as beyond the scope of

the Commission’s review of such filings.14


12
  Tariff, Schedule 12 further provides that customers designated to be responsible for assignments of costs
that PJM files with the Commission shall have 30 days from the date of such filing to submit comments
regarding the proposed cost responsibility assignments. Tariff, Schedule 12(b)(viii).
13
  PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 185 FERC ¶ 61,107, at P 24 (2023) (“November 2023 Order”) (citing PJM
Interconnection, L.L.C., 165 FERC ¶ 61,078, at P 20 (2018) (stating “PJM’s filing pursuant to section 205 of
the [Federal Power Act] to change the cost responsibility assignments in Schedule 12 Appendix A simply
reflects the result of the cost allocation method found in Schedule 12 of the Tariff”)). See also PJM
Interconnection, L.L.C., 191 FERC ¶ 61,156, at P 17 (“[W]e limit our review of the proposed revisions to
Schedule 12-Appendix A to determining whether PJM followed its Tariff provisions in assigning cost
responsibility for the proposed baseline upgrades.”).
14
   See, e.g., PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 189 FERC ¶ 61,160, at P 18 (2024) (“As the Commission has
previously stated, challenges to the PJM Tariff cost allocation provisions or the selection of transmission

appropriately raised through separately filed complaints and not through protests to the reports of cost
responsibility assignments.”) (footnote and citation omitted); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 187 FERC
¶ 61,012, at P 28 (2024) (“We review the proposed revisions to Schedule 12 Appendix A and Appendix C

citation omitted); November 2023 Order, 185 FERC ¶ 61,107, at P 24 (“As PJM noted in its answer, the

review PJM’s RTEP update filings to determine whether PJM appropriately followed its Tariff provisions in

the formula itself is unjust and unreasonable.”); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 178 FERC ¶ 61,113, at P 28
(2022) (same); 175 FERC ¶ 61,152, at P 47 (2021); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 152 FERC ¶ 61,187, at
P 25 (2015); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 147 FERC ¶ 61,028, at P 43 (2014) (“The reasonableness of the
solution-based DFAX methodology is beyond the scope of this proceeding.”); In re PJM Interconnection,
L.L.C., 139 FERC ¶ 61,242, at P 29 (2012) (“The issue at hand is whether PJM’s Filing complies with Order
No. 503’s directives,” not whether the merchant transmission facilities customer agreements allow for the
pass-through of RTEP costs or whether pass-through of RTEP costs to such customers is consistent with the
public interest.); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 139 FERC ¶ 61,010, at P 11 (2012) (determining issues raised
by the Illinois Commission are beyond the scope of the docket and the only issue is “whether PJM has
determined the cost responsibility . . . consistent with the methodology set forth in Schedule 12 of the PJM
Tariff”); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 135 FERC ¶ 61,044, at PP 20, 22 (2011) (finding that the ICC did not
state that the modeling assumptions used by PJM were inconsistent with the Tariff and, thus, further inquiry
into the modeling assumptions required by the Tariff is beyond the scope of this proceeding).



                                                      5
            In the August RTEP Cost Assignment Filing, consistent with the requirements of

Tariff, Schedule 12(b)(viii), PJM submitted amendments to Tariff, Schedule 12-Appendix

A to include proposed cost responsibility assignments for the 38 transmission facilities

approved for inclusion in the RTEP by the PJM Board on July 15, 2026.15 Notwithstanding

the clear Commission precedent described above limiting this proceeding to whether PJM

correctly applied the cost allocation provisions of its Tariff, Towering Concerns expressly

states that it does not believe that PJM has violated its tariff or applicable law.16 Yet it asks

the Commission “to analyze whether the process used was adequate to ensure accuracy and

whether further action is required,” and raises other objections concerning the projects and

their scope. Towering Concerns identifies no Tariff requirement that PJM failed to follow

in calculating the proposed cost responsibility assignments included in the August RTEP

Cost Assignment Filing. To the extent its objections seek review of matters beyond PJM’s

application of the Tariff, including the adequacy of PJM’s planning process or its

underlying RTEP decisions, those issues are beyond the scope of this proceeding. The

only issue in this proceeding should be whether PJM determined the cost responsibility

assignments included in the August RTEP Cost Assignment Filing consistent with the

Commission-accepted methodologies set forth in Schedule 12 of the PJM Tariff, not

whether a specific project’s need is still consistent with the earlier filing and order

accepting it or whether the project has the necessary site control or is properly located per

state regulation.17


15
     See August RTEP Cost Assignment Filing at 1, n.3.
16
  See, e.g., Towering Concerns Protest at 18-19. (“We don’t believe that PJM has violated its tariff or
applicable law, but we do ask the Commission to analyze whether the process used was adequate to ensure
accuracy and whether further action is required.”).
17
     Towering Concerns Protest at 7-18.



                                                     6
            Absent any evidence that PJM failed to allocate costs consistent with the

Commission-accepted methodologies set forth in Tariff, Schedule 12, the Towering

Concerns Protest should be rejected.                 PJM therefore respectfully requests that the

Commission reject the Towering Concerns Protest as outside of the scope of this

proceeding.

           B.       Change in Project Description Between March 2025 RTEP Cost
                    Assignment Filing and July PJM Board Approval

           Towering Concerns alleges that PJM’s August RTEP Cost Assignment Filing is

inaccurate with regard to b4000.344 and b4000.345 given that these projects were revised

in the May 2026 TEAC to include expanded scope and revised structures. Towering

Concerns notes that Dominion, the Transmission Owner with construction responsibility,

“told PJM [b4000.344 and b4000.345] would now cost an additional $60.5M. The PJM

Board approved the scope changes in July 2026.”18

           The July 2026 scope changes and associated cost increases do not, by themselves,

establish that the August filing was inaccurate. Although the PJM Board approved a scope

change for the Thornburg Project in July 2026, that scope change did not alter the project’s

cost responsibility assignments—which the Commission accepted in May 2025.19 Because

the July scope change resulted in no new or revised cost allocation assignments for the

project, PJM proposed no change to its existing Tariff entry.20 That said, PJM maintains

current project information for all projects included in the PJM RTEP on the Project Status



18
     Towering Concerns Protest at 5 (footnote and citation omitted).
19
     See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 191 FERC ¶ 61,156.
20
   PJM recognizes that the August RTEP Cost Assignment Filing could have updated the description
associated with projects b4000.344 and b4000.345 in Tariff, Schedule 12-Appendix A to correspond with
the revised project description. PJM will do so through a future clean-up filing.



                                                       7
 & Cost Allocation page of its website.21 Additionally, the May 2026 TEAC materials

describe the scope change, including the 230 kV underbuild capability, the revised

structure configuration, and the project’s estimated costs.22 Accordingly, PJM’s August

RTEP Cost Assignment Filing carried forward the project’s existing Tariff, Schedule 12 –

Appendix A entries; it did not propose a change to the project’s description or cost

responsibility assignment, which were unaffected by the Board approved scope change.

           C.       Towering Concerns Presents Incomplete and Inaccurate Representations
                    in Need of Correction

           Notwithstanding the narrow scope of this proceeding, PJM seeks leave to file this

answer to correct inaccurate statements in the Towering Concerns’ Protest and provide

useful and relevant information that will assist the Commission in its decision-making

process.        These corrections should not be construed as PJM acquiescing that this

proceeding is the appropriate venue to resolve the out-of-scope issues raised by Towering

Concerns Protest.

                    1.      Towering Concerns’ reference to PJM 100% site control is
                            inapposite

           Towering Concerns asserts that Dominion “does not have necessary site control to

construct” these projects.23 In support, Towering Concerns points to a Commission order

approving PJM’s Order No. 2023 compliance filing.24 Aside from timeliness and scope,

this claim lacks merit in several ways. First, Order No. 2023 and PJM’s compliance filing

23

24

                                                      8
 address generator interconnections and, as relevant here, site control requirements for

generators; they do not pertain to PJM’s identification of baseline transmission facilities

as the more efficient or cost-effective solution to a transmission need. Second, through

PJM’s Regional Transmission Expansion Planning Protocol (“RTEP Protocol”), PJM plans

for the transmission needs of the PJM Region. PJM does not site transmission facilities—

that is the province of the states.25 The RTEP Protocol includes no rules requiring an entity

to demonstrate site control before the PJM Board approves cost assignment responsibility

in the RTEP.

                    2.      PJM continues to evaluate whether approved projects remain
                            needed as conditions change

           Towering Concerns further alleges that the need for the Thornburg Project no

longer “accurately reflect[s] current conditions in the area.”26 It points to several anecdotal

references to declining data center demand and recent data center rejections or

cancellations in the area. Specifically, Towering Concerns contends that “data center

projects in Fredericksburg, Spotsylvania, and Stafford counties have been withdrawn,

reduced, delayed, or outright rejected,” since the Thornburg Project’s needs analysis was

completed in 2024, and argues that these changes may affect the assumptions underlying

the project.27 Towering Concerns asks PJM to require Dominion to “identify the specific

load forecasting assumptions justifying [the Thornburg Project] and explain whether those

assumptions remain current.”28



25
  See Transource Pa. v. DeFrank, 156 F.4th 351, 378 (3rd Cir. 2025) (“[T]he task of approving construction
in a particular place falls to state authorities.”).
26
     Towering Concerns Protest at 16.
27
     Towering Concerns Protest at 3.
28
     Towering Concerns Protest at 3.

         These concerns miss the mark. First, this proceeding concerns PJM’s application

of the Tariff’s cost allocation rules, not transmission planning.29 Second, the possibility

that individual load customers may modify or cancel their plans does not automatically

alter PJM’s assessment of need. The selection of a transmission project for inclusion in

the RTEP does not mean that PJM thereafter assumes that the system conditions underlying

that selection will remain unchanged. Rather, PJM continues to evaluate the reliability

need of the transmission system through subsequent RTEP analyses using updated system

conditions and assumptions, including changes in load, generation, transmission topology,

and other relevant system conditions—and may cancel a project included in the RTEP if it

was no longer needed.30

        Nor does PJM restart the original project selection process each time an individual

planning assumption or system condition changes. Major transmission facilities require

years to develop, site, and construct, during which the planning baseline necessarily

continues to evolve. PJM considers changed system conditions through its ongoing RTEP

analyses. If the cancellation or modification of a particular customer project results in a



29
   See, e.g., PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 189 FERC ¶ 61,160, at P 18 (“As the Commission has previously
stated, challenges to the PJM Tariff cost allocation provisions or the selection of transmission projects
included in the PJM RTEP pursuant to the provisions of the PJM Operating Agreement are appropriately

assignments.”) (footnote and citation omitted).
30
  See Am. Mun. Power, Inc. v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 191 FERC ¶ 61,001, P 39 (2025). In response
to paper hearing questions, PJM stated that it “has historically reevaluated the need for an RTEP project
regardless of whether a Designated Entity Agreement is in place, and if a project was found to no longer be
needed or progressing towards timely completion, PJM has replaced or terminated the project.” See PJM
Interconnection, L.L.C., 142 FERC ¶ 61,156, at P 6 (2013) (“PJM staff reviewed results of analyses showing
reliability drivers no longer exist for the MAPP Project throughout the 15-year planning cycle. After
considering PJM staff’s recommendation resulting from additional reliability analyses and communications
received from PJM stakeholders, on August 24, 2012, the PJM Board terminated the MAPP Project and
removed it from the PJM RTEP.”); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 141 FERC ¶ 61,177, at P 6 (2012) (“In
2011, PJM conducted additional analyses and concluded that due to decreasing customer load growth,
increasing participation in demand response, and the expected addition of new generation in the region, the
need for the PATH Project no longer existed throughout PJM’s 15 year planning horizon.”).



                                                   10
 material change to the system conditions underlying a previously approved transmission

facility, PJM’s subsequent RTEP analyses provide the mechanism for identifying the

reliability implications of that change and determining whether any corresponding change

to the previously-approved transmission solution is warranted.

       Thus, the cancellation of individual load projects does not, standing alone, establish

that the Thornburg Project is no longer needed. The Thornburg Project was selected to

address the reliability violations through the 2024 Window 1 process, underpinned by the

forecasted load growth projections and system conditions that PJM believes remain valid,

despite the subsequent project cancelations, and PJM will continue to evaluate the

reliability of the transmission system as system conditions evolve.




                                            11
 IV.     CONCLUSION

        For the reasons set forth above, PJM respectfully requests that the Commission:

(i) grant this motion for leave to answer; (ii) reject the arguments set forth in the Towering

Concerns Comments; and (iii) accept the Tariff revisions proposed in the August RTEP

Cost Assignment Filing, effective November 12, 2026.
